name: carolina pulled pork
instructions:
Carolina-style pulled pork. Dutch-oven braise of pork shoulder in an apple-cider-vinegar-and-chicken-broth base with brown sugar, worcestershire sauce, and red chili flakes. Tomato paste is OPTIONAL and marks the eastern-vs-western Carolina divide (see notes) — omit for Eastern-style (pure vinegar), include for Western/Lexington-style (vinegar + tomato).

SERVES 4-6. Dutch oven, 325°F oven.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 2-3 lb pork shoulder, cut into large chunks (~2-3 inch pieces for browning)
- 2 tbsp neutral oil (vegetable / avocado) for browning
- 1 white onion, chopped (goes in the braise — see notes)
- 1/2 cup chicken broth (or chicken stock)
- 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar
  (Total liquid ~3/4 cup, half-covering the pork. Adjust vinegar-to-broth ratio to taste — I skew slightly more broth than vinegar; a 50/50 split works too.)
- 2 tbsp brown sugar
- 1-2 tbsp worcestershire sauce
- 1-2 tsp dijon mustard (subtle nod to the SC mustard-based tradition without going full mustard — see notes)
- 1/2 tsp garlic powder
- 1/2 tsp red chili flakes (adjust to heat preference)
- salt and black pepper
- OPTIONAL (Western/Lexington style): 1-2 tbsp tomato paste — see notes

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREHEAT the oven to 325°F.

2. BROWN THE PORK: heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Season the pork chunks with salt and pepper. Brown on all sides — work in batches if needed (don't crowd or they'll steam instead of brown). Transfer browned chunks to a plate as you go.

3. SAUTÉ THE ONION (SAME POT): reduce heat to medium. In the fond left from browning, sauté the chopped onion until softened and starting to color, ~5-7 min.

4. BUILD THE BRAISING LIQUID: return all the browned pork to the Dutch oven with the onion. Pour in the chicken broth + apple cider vinegar so the liquid comes ABOUT HALFWAY UP the pork chunks (~3/4 cup total for a 2-3 lb shoulder — adjust up or down for pan size). Stir in the brown sugar, worcestershire sauce, dijon mustard, garlic powder, red chili flakes, and tomato paste if using.

5. COVER AND BRAISE: cover the Dutch oven and transfer to the 325°F oven. Cook 1-2 hours until the pork is fork-tender — should break apart easily when you press with a fork.

6. SHRED: remove from oven. Shred the pork with two forks right in the Dutch oven, tossing in the braising liquid + softened onion so the meat absorbs the vinegar-broth base.

7. SERVE: on buns, over rice, or on its own. Traditional accompaniments: coleslaw, pickles, cornbread ([[southern-style-cornbread]]).
notes:
Classic Carolina-style pulled pork — Dutch-oven braise (rather than smoked, which is the traditional method but requires equipment most home kitchens don't have). Vinegar-forward braising liquid keeps the meat bright and cuts through the pork shoulder's fattiness.

=== EASTERN vs WESTERN CAROLINA — THE TOMATO PASTE QUESTION ===

Carolina barbecue splits into distinct regional traditions on sauce composition:

- EASTERN CAROLINA (whole hog country): vinegar-based, THIN sauce, NO tomato. Just vinegar + red pepper flakes + salt + maybe a touch of sugar. The vinegar cuts the pork's fat and lets the meat's flavor lead. Omit the tomato paste for this style.
- WESTERN / LEXINGTON-STYLE (Piedmont): vinegar + TOMATO (either ketchup or tomato paste) + sugar. Slightly sweeter, thicker, more tangy-sweet. Include the tomato paste for this style.
- SOUTH CAROLINA (Midlands): mustard-based. Very different tradition, not what this recipe is going for.

The tomato paste is the single knob that swings you east vs west in this recipe. 1-2 tbsp tomato paste for Lexington-style; omit entirely for Eastern-style.

=== ONION IN THE BRAISE ===

Some carolina-pulled-pork recipes chop up a white onion and braise it alongside the pork — I've seen this as a common addition and it works well. Sauté the onion in the fond after browning the pork, then add it to the braising liquid. As the pork cooks the onion breaks down into the sauce, adding sweetness and body without leaving discrete pieces. When you shred at the end, the onion is already dissolved / broken into the sauce.

Don't need much prep — just rough chop, no need to dice fine (it's going to break down anyway).

=== DIJON MUSTARD — SUBTLE NOD TO THE SC MUSTARD TRADITION ===

1-2 tsp dijon mustard in the braising liquid is a subtle move that bridges toward the SOUTH CAROLINA mustard-based barbecue tradition without going full mustard-based (which would be a different dish — see EASTERN vs WESTERN note). The dijon reads as tang and depth rather than as a distinct mustard flavor — you don't taste 'mustard' in the finished pork; the mustard's fermented-tang character just adds a layer to the vinegar-forward base.

Same lesson as [[lentil-cottage-pie]] where dijon is 'confirmed as tested addition (adds tanginess without being tasteable)' — dijon in small amounts is a general depth-enhancer, not a flavor-forward ingredient.

=== GARLIC POWDER — STANDARD BBQ / BRAISE SEASONING ===

1/2 tsp garlic powder in the braising liquid. Standard barbecue seasoning — doesn't do dramatic work on its own but fills in the aromatic register cleanly. Fresh garlic would work too (2-3 cloves minced, added with the onion sauté) but powder is more traditional in the pulled-pork context and doesn't need any additional prep.

=== LIQUID RATIO — 3/4 CUP TOTAL, HALF-COVERING THE PORK ===

The liquid should come about HALFWAY UP the pork chunks — enough to braise but not enough to submerge them (submerged pork boils rather than braises). For a 2-3 lb shoulder in a standard Dutch oven, ~3/4 cup total liquid (~1/2 cup chicken broth + ~1/4 cup apple cider vinegar) is the right range. Adjust up or down based on your pan size and how much pork you're braising.

BROTH-TO-VINEGAR RATIO: 50/50 works. I tend to skew slightly more broth than vinegar (2:1-ish broth:vinegar in the 3/4 cup) — gives the finished sauce a rounder body while still keeping the vinegar's brightness. Straight-up half-and-half is fine too; pure-vinegar (Eastern-style purists) also works if you want maximum acid.

=== BROWN THE PORK FIRST — DON'T SKIP THE SEAR ===

The brown-in-oil step is where a lot of the finished flavor comes from. Fond stuck to the Dutch oven from the sear dissolves into the braising liquid and gives the sauce depth that a straight-braise-from-raw approach doesn't get. Work in batches if needed — crowded pork steams instead of browns, and you lose the fond.

=== SHOULDER IS THE CUT (BONE-IN OR BONELESS) ===

Pork shoulder (also called Boston butt) is the load-bearing cut for pulled pork. High fat content + connective tissue → slow braise breaks the connective tissue into gelatin and renders the fat, giving the classic pulled-pork texture. Loin or tenderloin cuts don't work — too lean, will end up dry and stringy.

Bone-in vs boneless: either works. Bone-in has slightly more flavor and a longer cook time; boneless is easier to cut into chunks and cooks faster.

=== 1-2 HOURS AT 325°F — CHECK FORK-TENDERNESS ===

1-2 hours is the range for the covered braise. Check at the 1-hour mark: if a fork breaks the pork apart easily, it's done. If there's resistance, continue in 15-30 min increments. Bigger chunks and bone-in cuts trend toward the longer end.

Don't over-braise — the pork will keep breaking down past fork-tender and eventually go stringy-dry. Pull it when a fork just breaks it, not when it falls apart on its own.

=== SHRED IN THE BRAISING LIQUID ===

Shred the pork right in the Dutch oven with two forks, tossing the shreds through the braising liquid so the meat absorbs the vinegar-broth base. If the liquid is too thin after shredding, you can transfer the pork to a plate and reduce the liquid on the stovetop for a few min, then toss back in.

=== SERVING — BUNS, RICE, OR CORNBREAD PAIRING ===

Traditional Carolina serving: on soft buns with COLESLAW on top (the slaw's crunch and creaminess balance the vinegar-braised pork). Also good over rice or with [[southern-style-cornbread]] on the side.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[southern-style-cornbread]]: traditional pairing on the side — the cornbread's savory-corn register complements the vinegar-pork.
- Other meat mains in the cookbook: this is the only pulled-meat-style braise so far.
